As Hans Christian Andersen told it, 1837
“Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower, and as clear as crystal, it is very, very deep.”
“The walls are built of coral, and the long Gothic windows are of the clearest amber. The roof is formed of shells, that open and close as the water flows over them.”
The Sea King had been a widower for many years. His old mother kept house for him, and she wore twelve oysters on her tail to show her high rank.
Walk up to the amber doors to go in: three floors of rooms, every one of them of the sea.
The Little Mermaid, by Hans Christian Andersen

“The youngest made hers round like the sun, with flowers as red as his rays at sunset.” She wanted nothing else in it but a marble statue of a handsome boy, found in a wreck, and she planted a rose-coloured weeping willow by it.
“Each of the young princesses had a little plot of ground in the garden, where she might dig and plant as she pleased. One arranged her flower-bed into the form of a whale.”
“Another thought it better to make hers like the figure of a little mermaid.”
Andersen names three of the six gardens (a whale, a little mermaid, and the round red sun). This sister chose the
Each sister was a year younger than the next. On her fifteenth birthday each was allowed to rise to the surface for the first time and see the world above.

the youngest daughter of the Sea King in Hans Christian Andersen's The Little Mermaid (1837), before her fifteenth birthday: quiet and thoughtful, who loves her round red garden, the marble statue in it, and above all hearing about the world above the sea. She has the loveliest voice in the sea. Never use any film or cartoon version; only Andersen's story
Oh! Have you come from up there? Tell me, is it true that the flowers have a scent, and the fish in the trees sing? Grandmother calls the birds fish, so that we will understand.
the herald at the Sea King's door in Andersen's tale: grand, kindly, proud of the palace
The King is at home. Mind the amber doors; they are older than the oldest wreck.
The merfolk of the Deep live in houses grown from shells and coral round a square where the bubbles rise.
Andersen wrote that merfolk live for three hundred years, and when they end they become foam on the sea.
Every house here can be walked into. Each family keeps it its own way.
a merfolk mother in the shell town of the Deep, busy and cheerful, raising four children and a pet seahorse
Mind the little ones, they dart about like sprats. Have you seen inside our houses? Go in, go in; nobody locks a door in Shellhaven.
an old merman net-weaver in the shell town of the Deep who has mended nets for two hundred years and loves telling the old tales of the sea
Two hundred years I've knotted nets, and I still learn a new knot from the young ones. Ask me about the Sea King's daughters; I knew their grandmother when she wore only six oysters.
The way to the Sea Witch
“She had to pass through the middle of these crushing whirlpools to get to the Sea Witch's domain.”
“Her house stood in the centre of a strange forest, where all the trees and flowers were polypi, half animals and half plants.”
Nothing here can hurt you: it is a dream, and the whirlpools only spin.
The Palace of the Ten Kings
feel the hot one and the cold one
The House of the Harbour Master
As Plato told it, about 360 BC

Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias tell of an island "larger than Libya and Asia put together", beyond the Pillars of Heracles (the Strait of Gibraltar), ruled by kings descended from the sea god Poseidon.
Its city was built in rings: three of water and two of land round a central hill. Bridges crossed the rings; a canal ran in from the sea.
Plato says it sank "in a single day and night of misfortune", 9,000 years before the time of Solon.
Most historians think Plato made the story up, as a lesson about pride and power. No trace of it has ever been found.
Walk in along the canal, cross the bridges, and every building can be entered.

Solon of Athens (about 630 to 560 BC), the great lawgiver and poet, who (Plato says) heard the story of Atlantis from the priests of Sais in Egypt and passed it down through his family to Critias. Wise, modest, curious. Be clear that the story comes from Plato's dialogues and that historians think Plato invented it
Greetings, traveller. In Sais, by the Nile, an old priest told me: 'You Greeks are always children.' Then he told me of this city. I wonder now if I dreamed it too.

a priestess of Poseidon at his temple in Atlantis, as Plato describes it in the Critias: proud of the silver temple and the god's statue, who loves explaining the rings, the springs and the laws on the pillar of orichalcum
Welcome to the citadel. Mind the golden fence: the old precinct of Cleito is within it. The god's temple is open to you; go in by the silver doors.
a charioteer who races on the great course that runs round the outer ring of Atlantis (Plato: a racecourse a stadium wide); cheerful, competitive, loves horses
The course runs right round the ring! A stadium wide. Want to know the trick to the turns? Hold the inside horse tight.

a modern underwater archaeologist dreaming of Atlantis, who explains honestly what historians think: that Plato probably invented Atlantis; that the eruption of Thera (Santorini) about 1600 BC and the fall of Minoan Crete may have inspired it; that the real Greek city of Helike sank in an earthquake in 373 BC and was found again in 2001; and that Ignatius Donnelly's 1882 book made Atlantis famous
Real or not, it's a wonderful story. Want to know what the evidence actually says? Spoiler: Plato might have been teaching a lesson, not writing a history.

🐚 Inside the Sea King's Palace. Two floors of rooms of coral, amber and pearl: the Throne Room, the Great Ballroom, the Grandmother's room with her twelve oysters, the princesses' rooms, the Seahorse Stables. Look for the ✨ cards. Walk out through the amber doors to leave.
The Chart Room of the Seas
The Room of Things from Above

🐚 Inside a merfolk house. Shell and coral, pearls for lamps, a clam for a bed, a warm vent to cook on. Look for the ✨ cards; the family's own workroom is at the back. Walk out of the round door to leave.

🦑 Inside the Sea Witch's house. Bone and dark rock, jars of strange things, the cauldron bubbling green. Andersen's witch is wicked but she keeps her word. Nothing here can hurt you. Look for the ✨ cards; walk out of the jawbone door to leave.

The bath, from the hot spring

🔱 Inside the Temple of Poseidon. As Plato describes it: a roof of ivory worked with gold, silver and orichalcum; the god in his chariot behind six winged horses; a hundred Nereids on dolphins; the golden kings; the pillar of the laws. Look for the ✨ cards. Walk out through the silver doors to leave.
The Room of the Azure Robes
The Hall of the Golden Kings
The Hall of the Hundred Nereids

🏛️ Inside the palace of the ten kings. Built, Plato says, by each king trying to outdo the last, "until they made the building a marvel to behold for size and beauty". The Throne of Atlas, the Council of the Ten, the Court of the Springs, the royal chambers above. Look for the ✨ cards.
The Gallery of the Ten Kingdoms
The Council of the Ten Kings

♨️ Inside the baths. Plato: Poseidon brought up two springs, one warm and one cold, and the kings built baths round them, some open to the sky and some roofed for winter, "for the kings, for private persons, and for women". Look for the ✨ cards.
🏃 Inside the gymnasium. Plato says the rings had gymnasia for men and for horses, and a racecourse a stadium wide that ran right round the larger ring. Look for the ✨ cards.
